utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Good morning. Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Miroslav Tadic, and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Just, I don't see the witness here. I'm ready to proceed, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we have the witness brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Lazarevic: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, Mr. Sarkanovic.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Today we'll resume our examination-in-chief and watching the video footage that we began yesterday. However, before we start with that, I forgot to ask you a question yesterday. I remembered when I looked through the transcript, and I saw that Judge Williams asked you something in connection with phone calls. On the 17th of April, in the morning, apart from the telephone conversation with the duty officer at the command of the 4th Detachment that you referred to, did you talk to anyone else on the phone on the 17th of April.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: May the counsel's other microphone be turned on, please, for the benefit of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agreed with the duty officer at the detachment that I should not go anywhere that day. I had three telephone conversations with my uncle, Borislav Maslic, and with Cvijan Marinkovic, my friend, and the third one was with Kemal Bobic. The conversation was about the situation on that day, and the information they had about the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I want to know more specifically is your conversation with Kemal Bobic. Did you call him? What did you talk about? Did you talk to his wife or only to him?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only spoke to Kemal. I asked him whether he knew what was going on in Samac. And when he told me that he didn't, I told him, roughly, that the main facilities and institutions in Samac had been taken over by specials from Serbia and the Serb police. I told him it would perhaps be a good idea for him not to leave home, because I had seen armed people in the open area outside my house, my building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were friends with Kemal Bobic?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I still am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Just one little detail that I wanted to clarify.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to add something, if I may. Yesterday, when you asked me, I provided an answer that was incorrect, and another answer that was only partly correct. If I may be allowed to set this right. I did analyse what I said yesterday, and I realised that one answer was inaccurate and that another answer was only partly accurate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question was about the name of the Hunters' Association. I said the name was Samac. It's actually the handball club's name, which I'm president of, and the Hunters' Association is called pheasant. So that was completely inaccurate. And the other question was what I did during the night between the 16th and the 17th of April. The part where I talked about clamour in the corridor outside my flat and seeing two of my neighbours, Milos Savic and Savo Savic. The inaccuracy consisted in the fact that it wasn't Savo Savic, but rather Dimitrija Djordjic, who lives in the flat just above mine. So the accurate answer would be Dimitrija Djordjic and Savo Savic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this clarification. Can we please proceed where we stopped yesterday, namely, watching the video. We interrupted our watching of the video here yesterday. What we can see in this image, and what we need to identify this for the sake of the transcript: You said this was used as the detention room.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, detention room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We can state for the transcript that -- can you see anything on the screen?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's gone. Okay. I have it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There are bars on the window, and to the left of the room there are two cells on which there is a door with bars. Does that -- is it consistent with what you know about this room?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just like you said it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time that you worked with the police, and during the time during the war that you worked there, has anything changed since in relation to what we're looking at now?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Go on with the tape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Lazarevic. Just before we move: Mr. Sarkanovic, the room that we have in front of us here, are the doors with bars? That's what it appears to be, the cells on the left, are they with bars?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, bars.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: And what I was wondering was: Yesterday you were saying, when we saw one of the offices, the room with the door open, the door that swung from left to right, you were saying that that room was used to detain quite a number of persons. Yes? I believe that's what you said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I'm just wondering: Have you any knowledge as to how it was decided which persons would be detained in a large group, in an office, versus those who were put into these cells with the bars? If you know, at the time, in April 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I said yesterday, I came into the office and they told me that Kemal Bobic, without really -- was there, without really knowing that there were other prisoners there. I don't know who ordered him to be kept there, and I'm not sure who decided who would be kept where, but I know that there were also a number of detained persons in the TO building across the way from the SUP building. There was a detention room, and I entered by accident. Well, perhaps not by accident, but I did stumble upon a group of perhaps about ten prisoners who were there together with Kemal Bobic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Okay. So if I understand you correctly, you don't know who decided which persons in the pictures that we're seeing on the video were put into an office room versus these cells we can see now with the bars.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, precisely. Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: An additional question on this same room. Does it mean that if a person is sitting on this stool we see on the right, he can see the prisoners inside the cell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't see any stool or bench.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. If I may just clarify [In English] He didn't have a picture on the monitor, so that was the problem.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. Yes, the person could see anyone inside these detention rooms. I think this is some sort of a desk, actually, used for work. It's not a bench. It's some sort of a small desk. I'm not sure how it got here, because usually it wasn't here in this room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We can now move on with the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can we stop now?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, the left-hand side of the image, you can see through the grid, through the bars on the window. What is that, exactly?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are garages that we used to store passenger vehicles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any people detained inside those garages at any point in time?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Dragan Lukac spent some of the time in these garages too.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Now we can move on with the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we just stop here, please. [In English] Can we stop now, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, what you can see now on the screen, can you identify this room?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the duty room reception desk, through which citizens speak to the duty officer, if they need to do something at the SUP.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we, therefore, agree for the transcript that this is the duty room or, rather, the duty officer's room?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just next to the staircase --

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's to the right of the staircase, leading up to the first floor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. You may remember - we talked about it yesterday, and today we've referred to it again - the room where persons detained at the SUP building were being kept and we looked at which way the door swung. This room that we have now referred to where detained persons were kept, if the door were opened between 10 and 15 centimetres, would you be able in any way to see the duty room from inside the room where people were being kept or the staircase?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There isn't half a chance, because the door of the office is perhaps between two and three and a half metres to the left of the staircase. As the door swings from left to right -- this is outside the field of vision of those looking from inside the office. The question is: Even if the door was wide open, would they be able to see anything unless they actually exited the room and came out into the corridor?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this explanation. That's all I wanted to know in connection with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Maybe we can go a bit faster, because this part of the tape is not particularly interesting. We'll have to go back. Sorry. Stop now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, we're still on the ground floor. These are the three offices. Further down the hall from the duty officer's room. Can you just tell me: Which three offices are these, really, and what were they used for?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The offices are on the right-hand side of the corridor, as you enter the SUP building. To the right there are two offices. Both were used for general and administrative affairs. To the left there is another office, which, before the war, was used for general and administrative affairs. During the war, it was used as an office of the commander of the police station, but you entered his office through another office, in which a police officer was sitting. So you had two offices there, and you went from one into the other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The precise spacial disposition is not that relevant at this point. We just wanted a general impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can we stop now and go a little bit back? Back, back. Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sarkanovic, obviously, we have gone up the stairs to the first floor. This seems to be the first office, with a padded door. We should perhaps state this for the transcript. And this is the first door you see once you climb the staircase to the first floor. Is that an adequate description of what we've seen?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me what this office is and who it was used by?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the war, this office was used by a police officer who was in charge of keeping records of the equipment that was used by the police station and the police officers would go to him to sign for their weapons or equipment. I don't think it was actually used during the war, at least during the time that I was there it wasn't used.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you see anything that's been changed as compared to the situation during the war? I'm referring to the padded door.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nothing's changed. But let me explain why it wasn't used. It's opposite a glass window which is on the landing of the staircase, with a view of Croatia. And as fire was being opened from Croatia, it was for fear of anyone getting hurt that the office wasn't used.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can we move on?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can we stop now?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, this is the corridor to the right of the first-floor landing. Can you please just enumerate the offices here in this part of the corridor?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first door to the right, the toilet. Straight and then to the right, communications room. Last door to the right is a door to the chief's secretary's room, through which you enter the chief's room, where, during the war, Todorovic was based. And prior to the war, the secretary who was in office at the time. They were changing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. When you said "communications room," is that where the man we referred to yesterday worked?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All communications officers worked there. They would make calls there, receive telexes, do their decoding, that sort of thing. The room has special insulation. It's soundproofed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The door where you can see the shoulder of a police officer sticking out, it's the lower left corner of the screen, what's that door?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the door to the office, which was used by the commander of the police station before the outbreak of hostilities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can we stop now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, we're on the left-hand side of the corridor now. We've reached the landing of the first floor. Now, to the right of us, and then from right to left, can you tell me about all the doors, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 doors, from right to left? Which offices are these and who were they used by?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first and second door to the right were doors to offices which, before the war -- which, before the war, were used by the crime department. The second door is the door to my office. And straight on, there's the door to an office also used by the crime department. And all three offices were interconnected, with internal doors inside the rooms. The first door to the left was an office used by the deputy commander of the police station, and the second door to the left is a conference hall, a conference room. The name speaks for itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Looking from right to left, the first, second, and third doors in the middle were actually offices used by you, as a criminal inspector; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. The first office to the right, that's where our typist was. The middle office, I used the office in the middle; and then the third door, the office behind the third door, was used by Milos Savic. However, for conducting interviews, I was often using conference room too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As we continue watching the tape, we'll see the inside of these offices, but this may be a good moment to ask you the following question: Simo Zaric, during that time, whenever he came to the police station, at the beginning of the war, did he actually have his own office?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When he conducted his interview with Tihic or other inspections, did he use any of these offices?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically, when he was talking to Tihic, he was using my office. I conducted my interviews in the conference room at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can we continue the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can we stop now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, what we're looking at now, this is obviously the second office on the left-hand side of the corridor, which you defined as the conference room.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the conference hall, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is the room you had in mind when you spoke about conducting interviews there occasionally, interviews with prisoners?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: We can now move on with the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can we go back a bit? Just a second. Just a little bit more, more. Stop.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, through the window, what can you see in this conference hall?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The right bank of the Sava River. Actually, both the right and the left banks of the Sava River. This is the northern part of the building. Across the Sava River is Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this is a view onto the border between Bosnia and Croatia on the Sava River?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Now we can move a little bit faster.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: A little bit faster. Stop. Can we go back a little bit, just a little bit, to see ... Okay. Stop now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, can you identify this room which is now on the screen? What is the entrance? To which room?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a room -- room first on the right looking from the staircase, and from this office, you go into my office, and the very same door exists, to lead you to this other office, into which you can go in directly through the door straight on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the office where you said the typist was, the first office of the crime department out of three?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. That's the office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can we stop now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, this is obviously a view from the window of that office. Can you tell us: What can we see through this window of the office?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Through the window you can see a building and the yard of the TO. To the right, this building was used for offices. The yard and the other buildings probably for warehouses. I don't know. I never went in there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we agree that the yard of the TO and the TO building can be seen very well through the window of this office?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it -- was it in this way that you saw the events that you spoke about? You said that people were beaten, that they were forced to beat each other.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Through my -- through the window of my office, you can have the same view, from my office, not from this one. It is the same view, but I saw it's the same position, it's the same view.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: That's okay. I think that we've finished with the tape. I don't believe there is anything more that is of interest for Mr. Zaric's defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir, for identifying these rooms and premises. I hope that now everyone will have a good picture of what this all looked like and what it does look like.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... from the Prosecution for this tape as evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There's no objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we have a number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The videotape is marked D44/4.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, let us go back to your work. We're still in April of 1992. You explained how it came about that you were working in the police, and you told us about a number of other things. Now, can you try and recall, as much as you can: Did you take statements from any other persons that you can remember, at this time, in April of 1992? Specifically, I'm interested in Izet Izetbegovic, Fadil Sabanovic.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible that I took this statement from Izet Izetbegovic, but I'm not certain. I certainly took the statement from Fadil Sabanovic, because he told me about the way and the location where they brought, two days beforehand, so that would be Wednesday, the 14th of April, 50 automatic rifles and some other weapons. So I took the statement from him, and then from Hasan Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does the name of Jusufovic tell you anything?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Jusufovic I think it was Ferid's son. I think -- he was a sweet shop owner. I can't remember his name. I know he was Ferid's son. Perhaps his name was Dzevad. I think it was Dzevad, son of Ferid. And many others. But that was 10, 12 years ago. If you showed me the statement, then I would certainly be able to recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not insisting now. Just to the extent that you can recall. We only find interesting what you can recall.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was Hadzialijagic, also known as Pop. I know that I spoke to him. Then there was a certain name called Arapovic. I know that he also gave a good, usable, useful data. So there were quite many of them, but I can't remember all of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Of course, we won't insist now on all of this. Sir, before this Chamber, a lot has been said, so it's not contested that at one point in the month of April there was a murder that was committed in the TO building, that this was committed by Lugar, and the person who was murdered, his nickname was Dikan. His nickname was Dikan. His name was Ante Brandic. What do you know about this? What can you tell us about this?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that day, I was not in the SUP. I think that happened in the afternoon hours. I know that one of the specials from Serbia killed a prisoner, a detainee, called Dikan. And on the same day, because of the safety of other prisoners, the other prisoners were then transferred by military lorries to Brcko, most probably. That's how I was informed by Milos Savic, the next day, in the morning, when I came to work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So on that day you were on present. You don't know the circumstances of how that happened and what was happening?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. I just heard that he had taken him out and just without any reason killed him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the next day when you came to the station, you heard this?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Milos Savic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let us now go a few days forward. At one point, a certain number of these people who were transferred to Brcko, they were brought to the police station in Bosanski Samac, in order to be interviewed by the Novi Sad television. Were you there at the police station? If you were, can you tell the Trial Chamber what you recall and what you then saw.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that day, I was at the police station. I think that Sulejman Tihic, Omer Nalic, perhaps Izet Izetbegovic, were brought. I was in my office when somebody, I think one of the policemen, brought him to the office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a moment. When you say "him," who do you mean?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean Sulejman Tihic. Probably because upon his request, because my office was opposite the office where this interview was recorded. When Sulejman came and we exchanged greetings and had a chat, he then asked me to try and protect him. If that's possible, that Simo Zaric should, not in so many words, but be as close as possible to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your impression? What was Tihic's condition? Was he afraid? Was he anxious?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was scared. He was very worried about his children, about himself, the children, the family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me the actual recording: You said that was in the office opposite yours. Were you present when this recording was done?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This recording was done not opposite my office but in the other part of the building, in the office that was used by the chief of the station, Stevan Todorovic. So it was to the left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Perhaps I misunderstood you, but perhaps your answer does explain everything. Were you present when this recording was done?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I was not. I was not even -- when Sulejman Tihic went to that office, I stayed in my own office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you don't know the details about what went on there when the filming was done, when the recording was done?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Lazarevic. I wonder whether we could get some clarification of the witness's answer which is on page 16, lines 7 to 12. I don't find that it makes a great deal of sense. I think maybe it's translation or maybe some words have been left out. Do you see -- it says: "I mean Sulejman Tihic (office) probably because upon his request because my office was opposite the office where this interview was recorded. When Sulejman came and we exchanged greetings and had a chat, he then asked me to try and protect him. If that's possible, that Simo Zaric should not, in so many words, but be as close as possible to him." It doesn't really make too much sense, at least the first part and the last part.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, obviously, because I also had the impression this it needs a little bit clarification.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So can you please tell us again. If you listen carefully to what Judge Williams said. First of all, he was brought to your office, Sulejman Tihic was brought to your office, is that correct, and you were sitting for a while in your office with him?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after that, he was taken to the office where this interview was filmed?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us: This office where the interview was filmed, was this opposite your office or not?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not opposite my office. It's on the other side of the building completely, that is, looking from the stairwell when you go upstairs on the right-hand side of the corridor, while my office is to the left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you said "opposite," you meant the opposite side of the corridor, not opposite exactly?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. It's on the western side of the building, while my office is on the eastern side of the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Is it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I think that's clear. What's obscure, though, still is the last sentence which mentioned Mr. Zaric, where he says, that's lines 10 and 11: "If that's possible that Simo Zaric should not, in so many words, but be as close as possible to him." It doesn't make any sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, maybe the translation was not quite precise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Do you think we could just clarify this?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I will try to clarify this with the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, can you tell me: What did Sulejman Tihic tell you in relation to Simo Zaric in the interview?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sulejman Tihic, when he said that, what he meant, because he trusted Simo Zaric and he felt safe if Simo was there. That's what he meant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he asked if Simo could be with him to be safe; is that -- I don't want to lead you, but is that what he meant? Is that what you meant to say?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I meant to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, because we're nearing the end of April, let us go into May 1992 and talk about some events that are of relevance for this case. We all know that in May, in early May, a crime in Crkvina was committed when Lugar killed 16 people who were in prison there. Can you tell us: What do you know about this event? What did you find out personally? Was there something that was -- any steps that were taken, any measures? What do you know in relation to this event?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that morning when I came to the police station, myself and Milos Savic were told by the commander of the police station that the previous night Lugar had killed 16 detained prisoners in Crkvina. When we learnt about that, we more or less wanted to go and conduct an on-site investigation, after which Milos Savic went to Stevan Todorovic, and after a while he returned. He said that we will not be conducting an on-site investigation, that that's what Stevan Todorovic had ordered. Of course, we didn't go there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me: When you said "we," who did you mean?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant the investigation team, myself and Milos and the criminal technician. I meant the team. I meant the team for the on-site investigation that is made up of the inspector and the forensic or the criminal technician, and of course the investigating judge if he's free, but at that time he was not from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me: How did you feel when the order came from Todorovic not to go to the on-site investigation?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What could we do? We had to obey, don't go, so we wouldn't go. Even when Dikan was killed, there was no on-site investigation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, just to be precise for the transcript. You mentioned that you heard that from the commander of the police station for that crime. Can you please give his name here so that we have that for the record.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of the police station was Mr. Savo Cancarevic, and he knew that because this prison in Crkvina, or perhaps the premises where the detainees were held, this was secured by the policemen. So he is the person who is the first one to find out about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Among the people who were killed in Crkvina - now their names are known - were there persons whom you knew personally?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were. Among them was the former chief of the Secretariat for Internal Affairs and the policeman and employee of the Secretariat for the Defence, Josip Orsolic, then Luka -- not Hrskanovic. I will probably recall. I know that these two were certainly among them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You knew them well?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only had I known them; I had worked with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will ask you about some other things that occurred in the month of May. Can you tell me, if you know anything about the taking away of a certain number of women from Samac to Crkvina and for their detention for a while?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything in particular. I know that from Samac, women were simply rounded up. There were Croatian and Muslim women that were taken for Crkvina, and they were held there for two, three, four days, and after that they were released.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know why this occurred? Who had decided this?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why. I don't know whose decision this was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I'd like to tell you something else in relation to this. Who rounded these women up in Samac and took them to Crkvina and detained them there? Which service did this?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There is one other thing I want to ask you about, and that is about a certain number of people who were detained in the school centre in Bosanski Samac, that is, in gymnastics hall in the school. Did you have any information about that? What kind of information? Where did you get it? Who did you get it from? Who were the people who were detained there?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had information. In fact, I had conducted interviews also with the people who had been detained there. So when a policeman would bring such a person, then, among other things, the first thing asked would be: Where were you? What was your accommodation? And so on. So that's when I realised that at the secondary school centre there were also premises that were used for detainees. Most of them were Croats from the villages around Samac, so Hrvatska Tisina, Hasic 1, Hasic 2, then Novo Selo, Zasavica. These were the only Croatian villages in the municipality of Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you had conducted interviews with these people, these Croats who had been detained in the secondary school centre. What were the circumstances when you conducted the interviews? Is this the same -- was it the same things that you asked in other interviews or were there any specific things?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the same, except what was known is that in those villages there had been a unit that had been established by the HDZ on the level of the battalion, and they had been made up of three infantry companies, one in Gornji Hasic, the second one in Donji Hasic, and one made by the locals of Tisina and Novo Selo. One part of the weaponry was handed over by these people, but the major part of these people took the weapons and they went through Novo Selo, Bazik, to Domaljevac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, obviously these were not the people who had gone via Bazik to Domaljevac. These were the people who remained, who had been arrested, that you had interviews with?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think - I can't tell you exactly - I think it was about mid-May that there was an ambush that was set up for the bus that was taking members of the JNA to the front line in Grebnice, on which occasion the wounding occurred of a large number of these members. Because of that, there followed this operation and detention of these people in order to shed some light on the events and also to gather some weaponry that had remained in the villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can the witness be shown Exhibit P18. And for the benefit of our clients, if it could be placed on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, can you please look at this document. There are three pages all together, this being the first. Can you look through the remaining two pages, please.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This document, have you ever seen it before?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw it at the SUP building. From this document, you can see which persons were abroad, which persons abroad or domestically, at home, gave contributions, that is money, that was later to be used for purchasing weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you now, please, look at page number 3 of this document.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I only have two pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: According to my records, this actually has three pages, and I checked this with the Prosecution as well. Because according to their records also, it has three pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: This is P18?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. The last page is ERN number 00457856.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, this document very much speaks for itself. It's about money that had been collected.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the way it was spent. You can see that a number of rifles were purchased, ammunition, that sort of thing. Yeah, I've seen the document before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Just one small detail on this balance sheet. The lower left corner, it says: "In Donji Hasic," isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Donji Hasic, March 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you also tell me, please: Donji Hasic is a village, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the south of the Bosanski Samac municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the predominant population of the village?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Croatian only. The village of Donji Hasic, Donji Hasic, Hrvatska Tisina, Zasavica, those were exclusively Croatian villages. In Novo Selo there are some Serbs, in Grebnice also there are some Serbs, but very few, and all the other villages in that area were Croat only.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you conducted interviews with Croats who had been detained at the secondary school centre in May, did you show them this document? If, for example, they were in Donji Hasic?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if they were from Donji Hasic. But the statements I took from those people contained data that are not in this document. But, for example, they -- I remember an old man who was there and who said that he had contributed a bull. I can't really remember, but if the statements are still there, copies of it, I think it should be there included in the statement. He said he had donated a bull as his own contribution.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Usher. I don't need this document any more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, just another couple of issues I'd like to ask you in connection with this that are pertinent to our case. Can you please tell us, roughly, and if you know: How many people exactly had been arrested and were kept detained at the secondary school centre?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I can tell you. As I said before, I never went there. But probably there were about a hundred people, more or less, in view of the size of those villages. But I don't know the exact number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There is no need to insist on this, if you don't. Obviously, you conducted interviews with a large number of people who had been detained, Muslims and Croats. There were, as you say, certain people whose names were on certain lists, whom you interviewed with regard to weapons. In your professional opinion, were there any people there, any persons who had been detained for no reason at all?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No reason at all for me means that a person has been detained without the person's name being on any of the lists or mobilisation charts. I'm talking about the units set up by the SDA. And there were a number of such persons whose names were not on any of the lists and yet they were detained, which leads me to conclude that there were certain arrests which were made for no reason at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your opinion, and in view of the fact that you knew quite a number of those people, who were the persons that had been detained for no reason at all? Give us specific names, if you can, please.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hasan Izetbegovic, Esref -- Dragan Delic, I believe. There are probably some other people too; it's just that I can't remember them now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. I will not pursue this. This name, Esref, I think it's referred to very often. Is this Zaimbegovic?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Esref Zaimbegovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Another question in relation to a number of issues and then we shall conclude our examination-in-chief. Do you know anything about women and elderly people being held in Zasavica during the war and that those people were mostly Croat and Muslim -- of Croat and Muslim ethnicity? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know that they were there. I'm not sure for how long, because I left very soon. I left Samac very soon. I know for certain that the father of the typist who used to work for the crime department before the war was also there, Fetis Mustafic and his wife, among others, but I know about those two for sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever go to Zasavica during the war?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know why those people had been taken to Zasavica?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. I don't know why they were taken there or on whose orders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, how long did you stay at the police station in Bosanski Samac as an inspector?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stayed until the 13th of June, 1962, when, on that morning, Mr. Stevan Todorovic --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me. Just an obvious mistake in the transcript. You said 13 June 1962?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I meant 1992. It was a slip of the tongue. 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please: What happened exactly on the 13th of June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That morning when I came to work, outside in the corridor, the chief of the police station, Stevan Todorovic, told me that I was no good for that job, that I should no longer come to work, which I greeted with quite some joy. This gave me an opportunity to go back to the military unit, in which I spent the remaining time, the remaining period of the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you take this when Todorovic told you that you were no good for the job? I mean, you had been a police inspector for 20 years.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On several occasions, Stevan Todorovic suggested or hinted how I should go about my work with prisoners, how I should interview them. I disagreed and I did not follow his suggestions or instructions, and that was probably why he made that move.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said process, actually, and in the transcript it says "interviews." What did Todorovic mean by "process"?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He meant that prisoners were actually to be beaten and that force was to be used.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you went to a military unit, in which you stayed until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just another question: During your stay at the police station between the 19th of April and the 13th of June, how often did you meet Simo Zaric? Was that every day or only in certain periods? Can you please try to give us a general impression of how often you saw Simo Zaric throughout that period.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is very difficult to quantify. In the first days, Simo used to come more often to the police station, and then less and less, increasingly. And towards the end of my time at the police station, I think I no longer even saw him. Not so often. At the beginning, it was a bit more often, perhaps every two or three days, sometimes even two days in a row, and then at a later stage he only came very rarely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you did see him, would he spend the whole day at this police station?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, not the whole day. I think the only time he stayed the whole day is when he took Sulejman Tihic's statement. He didn't come at the same time, and so on. Sometimes earlier, sometimes later.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I have a couple of questions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: -- for this witness Cross-examined by Mr. Pantelic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Sarkanovic. I'm counsel Pantelic. I defend Mr. Blagoje Simic before this Tribunal. I have a couple of questions to ask you which relate to Blagoje Simic's defence. Mr. Sarkanovic, please tell me: I can't seem to remember. How long were you an active police officer? When did you retired?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 30th [phoen] of June, 1987

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's a small town, so I heard that you were quite a successful officer and held in high esteem. Tell me: Did you know Dr. Blagoje Simic throughout that period prior to your retirement?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very briefly, please: What was his past at that time? Had he ever been arrested? Did he have any record in terms of offences against public order?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. He was never arrested. He was a well-respected citizen of Samac and Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Pantelic. I think we've got an error as to the date of retirement once again. The answer on line 13, page 28 this time is 30th of June, 1987.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I heard, 1987, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, sir: In connection with the question by my learned friend and colleague, Mr. Lazarevic, you worked between mid-April and the 13th of June, 1992. Can you tell me, please: You've described the circumstances, the lists containing names of members of the SDA and the HDZ. The activists from the Croatian villages. Can you try to think back, please, because it's been a long time, but we could really use this information. In that period, roughly, how many statements did you take on the basis of these interviews? Five, ten, fifteen, thirty?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between 50 and a hundred, I'd say. Certainly between 50 and 100. I can't even give you an approximation, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I fully understand. I wasn't -- I didn't mean to insist. Tell me: How many inspectors, full-fledged inspectors, were there at the police station at that time when you worked, authorised inspectors, between April and June 1992? How many other authorised inspectors were there taking statements from persons?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In addition to myself, there was only Milos Savic, but later, when I left, I was replaced by Simo Bozic, who I can't say with any degree of precision, but I think he probably did the same kind of job that I had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I interrupted you. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Simo Bozic sometimes came even while I was there, but as far as I know, he did not take any statements.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you try and recall this, please, because you did work on a daily basis with Milos Savic, who was your superior: How many statements did he take throughout that period, roughly?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I really can't. I'd be guessing. But throughout that period, Milos had other duties too. He was in touch with the head, with the commander, which was not part of my job, which means that at the time, I had more time to devote myself to my work, to the interviews. Milos Savic, I'm not sure how long he stayed eventually, but I suppose he stayed for a much longer time than I did. So probably the number of his interviews is eventually much higher than those that I had conducted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In order to assist the Trial Chamber, because they may not be familiar with our legal system prior to 1992, Mr. Sarkanovic, tell us, please: Was this according to law? Was this in line with law, for a police body to take statements as part of the pre-trial proceedings? Was this based on law?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was perfectly lawful, and this is the way it had been done before the war, the same way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In view of your experience, tell us: Was it legal for the lawyer representing the person being interviewed to be present at the police station while you were taking the statement?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Criminal law rules out this possibility. It doesn't exist. And that's exactly the way it had been done before the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it sound fair if I suggested the following: You've tried to explain this, of course, but now I'll give you an opportunity. I'm talking about the following: In mid-April 1992, there is an atmosphere of insecurity in the town. There are shoot-outs and hostilities, are beginning to break out. Civilians don white armbands on their own initiative in order to protect themselves because they've seen members of military units do the same thing. Is this a fair suggestion what I'm putting to you now?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I said the same thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain, please.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sarkanovic, did you ever hear through the media -- did you ever see any posters or billboards about the town to the effect that from mid-April 1992 onwards, the non-Serb population should wear white armbands in Samac?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, you had said that you had two questions. You are over. And I can see that you are moving into the general areas, nothing specific to your client's defence. So please sit down.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have just two more issues, and I will finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. Please sit down. You did say you had only two questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, yes, I understand. But Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can you sit down.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Just for the record, can I submit -- can I give my submissions, I mean for the record, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well, since my client is charged on count 1 for the persecution, including the alleged violation of human rights of non-Serb population in Samac, I deeply believe and I firmly believe that all these events, especially when we heard the theory of Prosecution case that Crisis Staff and other municipal institutions where my client was the, I would say, president, imposed certain regulations with regard to the violation of the human rights of non-Serb population, including white armbands, allegedly, and some other things. That's why I think that all my questions were strictly and closely related to the charges against my client. So I'm not challenging Prosecution case with regard to the certain specific actions of my client. It's rather his alleged position in the terms of aiding and abetting, because that's why -- that's what the Prosecution up to now are claiming. So I think that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber is of the view that you have had sufficient opportunity to cross-examine on those issues, and you did call your witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, but, Your Honour, since --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can you sit down.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Because he's a policeman, Your Honour, and this is the first policeman that I have opportunity to cross-examine with regard to the subcharge --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The Trial Chamber is aware that he's a policeman. Can you sit down. Yes, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The Prosecution does not object to Mr. Pantelic completing a reasonable cross-examination if he feels there are areas necessary for his defence to put to this witness, and we place on the record that, as a matter of fairness, we don't object if there are matters which reasonably need to be explored. And he has said there are two more matters that he wishes to explore, and we certainly don't object to him doing that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic. The Trial Chamber, after consultation, and in view of what the Prosecution has said, we will allow you two more questions. Two more questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I'm deeply grateful to my learned friend from the Prosecution side in helping me to perform my duty as a counsel and to defend my client, and also I'm grateful to the Trial Chamber for the reconsideration of the previous ruling. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sarkanovic, do you have any personal knowledge as to Dr. Blagoje Simic ordering interviews of persons at the police station, or their arrest, or these persons to be brought in? Do you have any personal information on that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. I don't think I even saw Mr. Blagoje Simic, even outside, about town, let alone the SUP building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've explained that you attached your personal notes concerning your observations to statements speaking about people arming themselves on the 17th of April. Can you tell me, please: Was there any official investigation inside the MUP - and I'm referring to the MUP as the Ministry of the Interior - into omissions or mistakes committed by officers at the expense of prisoners? And I mean beatings. Were there any criminal proceedings against those who had abused police authority? Do you know anything about that? Did you learn anything about that while you were there at the police station?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not as far as I know, but charges were brought against assistant commander -- by assistant commander Milan Jekic because a police officer had abused someone and slapped someone. That's the only thing I knew about.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I've finished with my cross-examination. I'm very grateful to the Trial Chamber for allowing me this opportunity. [Interpretation] Mr. Sarkanovic, thank you very much again for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No further questions for this witness, no. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's 10.28, Your Honour. Would it be appropriate to take the break and for me to start at 10.58.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. We'll take our break and continue our proceedings at 1100 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Judge Lindholm is unable to sit with us, and we'll continue our proceedings understood Rule 15 bis, paragraph A. So the Prosecution can go ahead. Cross-examined by Mr. Re:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, my name is David Re. I'm going to ask you some questions for the Prosecution. You understand that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I just check with you the pronunciation of your name so I get it correct. Can you just say it slowly for me, please.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vladimir Sarkanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sarkanovic. Thank you, sir. Now, in 1991 and 1992, Mr. Zaric, whom you had known for many years, was in a position to know what was happening in Samac in relation to the arming of people, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was public -- an open secret. People were armed in a way that the Secretariat for the Defence mobilised a reserve force and armed them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, in his capacity, was in a position to know about the arming activities of all ethnic groups and all parties, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possible. I can't say for sure whether he knew or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I said he was in a position to know because of his role, the work he did in 1991 and 1992.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about the position, but it still could have happened that he didn't know. You understand? Because I was a police inspector, and there are many things that I didn't know. And I perhaps should have known.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You know that Mr. Zaric gave three statements to the Prosecution, don't you?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you've seen -- or you've had a chance to look at each of those three statements he gave to the Prosecution in April and June 1998, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. Your Honours, just a small intervention. The question of the Prosecutor whether the witness knew that Mr. Zaric had given three statements to the Prosecution, the witness stated: No. And the answer of the witness is in the transcript entered as being yes, which is then demonstrated further, but the further of the answer of the witness to say he had not seen these statements. I'd like this to be clarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe we go back to the question, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I will certainly clarify that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Perhaps the witness's microphones can be adjusted please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can the microphones --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: To assist my colleague, maybe the witness could come closer to the microphones, because this would probably avoid any misunderstanding of his answers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, of course, in 1992, was in a position to know who was responsible for the takeover of the municipality of Bosanski Samac, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he did know or whether he didn't know. He didn't tell me anything about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you about his position --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Can we just go back to this question where Mr. Lazarevic said the answer was actually no, not yes, about whether or not the witness knew about the statements which Mr. Zaric gave to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I will. I only ask the question because of information I had been given by -- we had been given by counsel from the other side. If it's incorrect, I'll clarify it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct -- I withdraw that. Are you aware that Mr. Zaric gave three statements to the Office of the Prosecutor in 1998?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown P142 ter. Can you please just show the witness, Mr. Sarkanovic, the first page, just the heading. You can see that that's an interview, a record of interview by Mr. Simo Zaric on the 3rd of June, 1998, to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please turn to page 22 of the record of interview. Can you just please read about halfway down, the English says "John." "So who was responsible for the takeover of Samac?" And the response, several lines down, is: "The Crisis Staff and the SDS, the authorities were responsible." You can see that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see the text in English, which I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Has the witness got P142 ter, which has got both English and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: There's one that has both Serbo-Croat and English.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's on page 22.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can see it now. Yes, it's here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want to direct your attention to where it says "John." "Who is responsible for the takeover of Samac?" The answer, with a bit of interpretation in between: "The Crisis Staff and the SDS, the authorities were responsible." Question: "The Crisis Staff were responsible?" Please read. And the answer, over the page: "That is my --." Just -- one. The answer: "That is my deep conviction, and I think the part of the responsibility can also be taken by the command of the 17th Tactical Group." Can you see that there, those questions and answers?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see the questions and the answers. But I have already said at previously asked question, that in the night between the 16th and the 17th, the key facilities were taken by the specials from Serbia and the Serbian police. I don't know. Perhaps maybe Zaric was in a position to know what he stated, but I don't know about that. I was not in his position to know this, what he is talking about here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, sir. Can you please listen carefully to the question and answer only that question and not another one. The question I asked you was: Can you read those questions and answers? You can. Please don't go on to other explanations. If there's anything that needs clarifying, Mr. Lazarevic will ask you afterwards. All I'm saying to you is that I want you to be aware that that is what Mr. Simo Zaric told the Prosecutors was his view as to what happened in 1992. That's all. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood that. I can see that here, from the statement, after I read it, but before I didn't know this.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can the witness now, please, be shown P140 ter, again the English and B/C/S record of interview with Mr. Zaric of the 1st of April, 1998.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, can you see on the front page, just so you know what you're looking it, it says: "Simo Zaric interview on 1st of April, 1998, Wednesday." That's the heading of the document, so we're sure we're looking at the same document.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please turn to page 28, the top of page 28. This is what Mr. Zaric said to the Office of the Prosecutor on the 1st of April, 1998, in relation to the arming of the three sides at that time, in April -- in 1992: "Not only them, but also other nationalist parties, wherever there were signs that they could provoke a terrible war. Now that you ask the question of defence preparation, yes, according to our information, our service had information that there were special armies and police instructors who did come to these nationalist parties in order to instruct them in the context of preparing for defence, and all three parties equally SDS, HDZ, and SDA, equally dirtied their hands in this." Do you see that question and answer there? That's at the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it. I read it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just read the remainder of the page in B/C/S to yourself, please. You've read it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please turn the page to page 29. The word "absolute would know" is at the top, then a question from the Prosecutor, Ms. Paterson: "Why don't you tell us a little bit more of what you did to learn about the collection of weapons and actual preparations for war that were being made by all three parties that you have mentioned: The SDS, the HDZ, and the SDA?" Which the answer is in part, the first part: "Now, the first signs were noticed in the field by the service and both by the public security service and the state security service since they were working together and this is when the links were established." You've read that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please just read the balance of the page to yourself.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please turn to page 30. About two-thirds of the way down, you'll see a question next to the word "Nancy." That's the Prosecutor: "And what about the SDS? What weapons were they collecting and how were they preparing for the war?" To which Mr. Zaric's answer was: "Now, of course that the legal gathering, collecting, acquiring of weapons was intensified when the war started in the territory of Croatia, and it was not only Croats who went to Croatia; it was also Serbs who went to fight in Croatia, to the area of Vukovar and Kninska Krajina, or another link existed here, that was a link, the SDS members, if nothing, were more -- in nothing, even more obvious this their actions as to what they were doing and taking weapons than some others. In a way, also I could see that the way they went into the field was the most obvious of all, but the scenario for going into the field, coming back with weapons was very similar for SDS and HDZ. A great number of them managed to acquire weapons, armed themselves through the reserve police force, because all three parties wanted to have as many reserve police as possible." You agree that what I've just read to you is the question and the answer by Mr. Zaric that he gave in that interview?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: May the exhibit be returned. Thank you, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to say something.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Not at the moment, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not know to such an extent like Mr. Zaric, considering that he was a member of the service, that in any case was dealing with this while he was working there. They were dealing with this. But as far as my knowledge goes, I don't know that much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fair enough. So you would agree that Mr. Zaric was not only in a position to know, but from what you've just read, did in fact know, with a fair degree of detail, what was happening in Bosanski Samac prior to April 1992?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very possible. I allowed for the possibility that he may have known about this, but I don't know what he knew about this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your evidence was yesterday that you had received a law degree I think in 1966 in Zagreb. That was your first degree. And you worked in law enforcement in 1969 until -- was it 1986 or 1987, when you retired?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters didn't hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were politically active during that time as a member of the League of Communists; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I worked as a police inspector, but I was a member of the Communist Party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your evidence over the last day or so has been of your awareness of many, many people being detained in Bosanski Samac after the 16th or 17th of April, and many of those people being mistreated while in detention. You agree with that, that that was your evidence?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with that, but I cannot tell you for sure how many people there were, because, as I said, I never went into these premises. I presume that there were many. I don't know what you mean by "many" or "a large number." I also said that most of these detained were physically mistreated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your evidence has been that Serb paramilitaries took control of the municipality or town of Bosanski Samac on the night of the 16th and 17th of April, 1992. That was your evidence, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From the 17th of April, 1992, the Serbs, or Serb forces, controlled the municipality of Bosanski Samac, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One part of the Bosanski Samac municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They controlled the town of Bosanski Samac and Crkvina and Zasavica, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These Serb forces that controlled that part of the municipality controlled the police, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether they controlled the police. My superior was Stevan Todorovic, and as far as I was concerned, he was the one who controlled me and my work. He and Milos Savic. Milos Savic being my direct superior.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I'll go back a step. The Serb forces that took control of the municipality on the 16th and 17th of April, 1992, after that date controlled the military forces in that area, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The army was separate, and these forces that had taken control of the town and certain facilities in the town, I said these were specials from Serbia and the Serb police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I could put it this way: It's correct to say that Serb forces, forces in the control of Serbs, controlled Bosanski Samac, the part you've discussed, after the 17th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those Serb forces in control included police, army, paramilitary?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not the army. I presume, considering the position of Stevan Todorovic as part of the structure of the authorities, they probably controlled the police but not the army.
