The army was under the command of the commander of the 17th Tactical Group. He was the only one who could have had the authority to give orders to the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Serbian -- sorry - Serb police and the specials, as you've called them, took control of the town on the 17th of April and took control of all organs of government, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They controlled the radio station, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I presume. That's also a very important facility, so they probably also controlled the radio station, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They controlled the two schools, that's the primary school and the secondary school, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The schools were empty. There were no teaching, no pupils, no teachers. They could have controlled those as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in the last three answers of the witness, I saw that on page 44, line 2, the army said -- the witness said: "I presume." And again in line 12, he also said: "I presume." And again he said: "I presume." In three answers now we can see that this is just guesswork by the witness, and I suggest that this should be struck from the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Re, you can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I can certainly attempt to clarify it, if it's important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These -- the Serb forces that -- or Serb police and specials that took control of the town, after they took control of the town, a Serbian or Serb Crisis Staff was in control of the organs of government, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I should imagine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, a moment ago, drew attention to the fact that you had said "I presume" and "I should imagine." When you just said "I should imagine," can we take it that you're actually saying: Yes, a Serb Crisis Staff was established and was in control of - just hang on - the organs of government in Bosanski Samac after the 17th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that this was possible, but I'm not sure if this was indeed the case. I assume so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, in your own words, Mr. Sarkanovic, who was responsible for garbage collection in Samac after the 17th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The council.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was responsible for running the hospitals?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Your Honours. A correction. The witness's answer was: "Communal services," not "council."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Re, can we just ask the witness what was his answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your answer to who was responsible for garbage collection, was that "communal services"?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's an organisation of labour, which is in charge of tidying up the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was responsible for hospitals and health?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The director of that institution, of the health centre, or of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Just one correction, and I would say a suggestion and an intervention. It is page 46, line 4. The witness said "radna organizacija" [phoen]. In order to clarify that, radna organizacija means company, simply as that. But according to the terms in previous legal system, he used that. So it cannot be said "organisation of labour." It's very vague. It's very imprecise. So maybe it should be clarified in that sense. Because company is one thing and organisation of labour is, I believe, nothing. So maybe it could be clarified or corrected. Maybe it's just my friend's suggestion to my learned friend from the interpreters when these terms are used, that's the old terms from socialist regime. It's simply company. It's company, nothing more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Re, you can go over that, if you think it's important to your case.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No, I don't disagree with Mr. Pantelic. I accept what he says.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: In fact, Mr. Re, if I can just make one little intervention. Maybe it would be better if we moved away from things such as garbage collection and talked about things which we know the Crisis Staff was involved in, civilian protection and so on and so forth, rather than that maybe dealing with something such as that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I will do that. If Your Honour could just excuse me for one second.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sarkanovic, on the 30th of October, 1990, there were democratic elections in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and in the municipality of Bosanski Samac, a multi-ethnic parties were elected to the Municipal Assembly, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after the 17th of April 1992, the democratically elected municipality of Bosanski Samac was no longer in power in the municipality, was it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Its place had been taken by the Serbian Assembly of Bosanski Samac, hadn't it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the Serbian Assembly didn't meet at first because it had a Crisis Staff which was performing all functions of the Serbian municipality in conjunction with an Executive Board?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this Crisis Staff, that's in April, May 1992, was performing the role of the Serbian -- sorry, of the former Municipal Assembly in taking over all of its functions, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the Crisis Staff was responsible for things such as the economy, the running of the economy in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what follows from that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Humanitarian and medical care?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Information and propaganda?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Crisis Staff, probably.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Procurement and food supplies?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Crisis Staff had taken over all the obligations and duties of the Assembly and the Executive Board, and that would have been that. They were responsible for everything. If so, again, because I'm not sure about the exact areas of competence of the Crisis Staff or the Executive Board. I can only assume what they would have been.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this answer, this whole series of answers, the witness is asked to speculate. I think we should decidedly demand that the witness speak about facts, and we have a whole line of answers here where the witness is speculating, as he himself has said. I think we're getting nowhere. The witness must be faced with facts, and then the witness will tell us whether he's familiar with these facts or not. This way, we are merely speculating, and I think that's the only place this line of questions by the Prosecution is leading to. I have nothing against specific questions, but for the second time in a row, the Prosecutor goes back to the same line of questions, receiving the same answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I've asked very, very specific questions. The witness has answered some of them positively and others I assume that it must follow from that. The witness is fully aware of what the functions of government was in Bosanski Samac. He worked for the government a long time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. And he knows that if he doesn't know, he can say so. And in fact in examination-in-chief he would answer like that, if he didn't know anything when questioned. So the Prosecution can continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Municipal Assembly, the previous one, the democratically elected one, had also been responsible for refugees?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which body it was that was in charge of refugees. I suppose the bodies of the executive government would have appointed someone or that there had been a decision by the Assembly governing such situations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Communication, another responsibility of the Municipal Assembly, taken over by the Serbian Assembly and the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've said, if the Crisis Staff had taken over the duties of the Assembly as defined in the period before the war, that means they would have taken over all of these tasks. I'm saying if that was the case. I was not in a situation to find out from first-hand experience, because I was not close to where these things were actually happening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The municipality had also been responsible for the safety of the population and property, hadn't it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was another function which the Serbian municipality took over from the elected municipality, and when it wasn't meeting, the Crisis Staff took over that function?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say you assume, you mean you assume because it logically follows that it being something the elected Assembly did before, if the Serbian one took over, it had to have taken over that particular function and the Crisis Staff in its place?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, precisely. Precisely. I don't know, however, if this really was the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After April 1992, a new system of government had been instituted in Bosanski Samac municipality, hadn't it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The authorities, the Serbian authorities in Bosanski Samac, had somehow had arrested many, many non-Serbs immediately after the takeover, hadn't they?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they had done so as part of the new system of government that had been instituted, the new regime?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know in which context that was, but, yes, it did happen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this new regime or new system allowed the mass arrest and detention of many, many non-Serbs immediately after the takeover, didn't it? I think you just said yes in English; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. No, no. I said yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which means yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just didn't hear what you said. I heard two things. Thank you, Mr. Sarkanovic. And this new regime or new system, which had ordered or allowed these mass arrests, also tolerated or permitted or allowed the people who had been arrested to be detained in horrific conditions in a number of detention centres, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conditions were like that. However, whether the Crisis Staff knew about that or not, I really can't say. I don't know. The conditions were indeed such as you have described.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Someone must have ordered these arrests and prepared the facilities for detention; you agree with that? Just yes or no. Please confine yourself. Someone must have done so, mustn't they?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I can answer like that. The facilities had been prepared. The secondary school was empty. The TO building was empty. And someone had to. That's right. But if you ask me, it was Todorovic, because he was the one who was most frequently ordering arrests. The commandos, members of special units, did it on their own initiative, or they had agreed with him to do that. I don't think any facilities had been specially prepared for that. They were as they were, and at the time they happened to be empty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you're aware, in your many, many years of experience as a police inspector, that if people are to be detained, there have to be facilities available for them at the time of their detention?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know from the video footage, because you could see that there were such facilities at the SUP for persons being detained. I think I understood your question. Yes, conditions needed to be met.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were aware of four detention facilities in Bosanski Samac: The secondary school, the primary school, the TO, and the SUP?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The elementary school was set fire to on the first day of the conflict. It was set fire to. It burnt down to the ground, literally. So the facilities where detainees were being kept were the secondary school building, the TO building, and the SUP building. The elementary school building had burnt down. That's for sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the gym of the primary school, Mr. Sarkanovic?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think I was talking about the secondary school gym. That's what I knew. I know it for a fact that the elementary school building burnt down to the ground, literally, on the first night of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, what I'm suggesting to you is that these detention centres didn't spontaneously appear. To detain people, you have to have facilities available and ready for the detention. You have to agree with that, don't you? Just as a simple proposition, you have to agree with that.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Facilities were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But, sir, it requires --

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with you, but the facilities were there already, and they were merely used for the purpose. Nothing special had been prepared, or at least not that I was aware of, but I know that the TO building and the secondary school building were simply empty. There were no pupils, students, or teachers there at that time, and these buildings were merely used for the purpose because they were convenient. I don't think there had been any special preparations for that, because there would have been no need for any such special preparations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sarkanovic. With respect to the primary school, which was burnt down: Is it true that the gymnasium building was a separate structure, not connected to the classroom areas that were burned down, to your knowledge, as a person who has lived in Bosanski Samac for a long time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My wife worked as a teacher at that school. The gym hall is in a wing of the school, in the western wing of the school, and this gym may not have burnt down. I'll allow for that. But believe me, I don't know. The main body of the building, or rather, the southern side of the building, there is the east and the west - the building is in that shape. So the central part was certainly set fire to and it certainly burnt down. The gym may have remained intact. I may not know, but I'm not familiar with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may just be allowed to add: When I spoke to the prisoners, none of them ever told me that they had been detained at the elementary school building. They all said the TO building, the secondary school building, or the SUP building.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There are some photographs in evidence, Exhibit 14A. The Prosecution doesn't have a copy in court of those. Perhaps if I could have access to the Registry copies of the photographs, I might be able to resolve that issue a bit later. Mr. Weiner will look at it. 14A -- P.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sarkanovic, if you don't quite understand what I'm saying, please ask me to clarify. When talking about facilities, I'm talking about the overall treatment and detention of the prisoners, not just the facility itself. Do you understand that? Do you understand what I'm saying?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you a simple question. I just want a simple answer, please. Did Bosanski Samac have detention facilities apart from those in the SUP before the 17th of April, 1992? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you see, to house the hundreds and the evidence in this case is uncontested that hundreds of people were arrested after the 17th of April, 1992, something had to be done to feed, clothe, and look after these prisoners; you agree with that simple proposition?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the Serb authorities that took control of the town after the 17th of April were the only ones who could have put into place the system for looking after the detainees, that is, feeding them, providing them with bedding, if they got bedding, clothing, and sanitary facilities; you agree with that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There were only about 30 -- between 30 and 50 special Serbian paramilitaries or commandos in the town, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many do you say were there?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Between 15 and 30, I would say. I don't know the exact number, but certainly not as many as you said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fifteen and thirty special Serbian paramilitaries or commandos would not have been able to staff, as you say, three, but there's evidence here of four, detention centres, guard hundreds of prisoners, feed them, clothe them, provide them with sanitation. That wouldn't have been physically possible, would it, for 15 to 30 people to do that, in four separation locations in the town?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't the commandos who stood guard around those facilities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, no. A moment ago, a few moments ago, you said you thought they were the ones who set up the facilities. All I'm saying to you: 15 for 30 people would not physically have been able to look after three or four detention centres -- can I finish the question? Can I finish the question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I object. I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can I finish the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Right at this moment, that is absolutely not what the witness said, that they were establishing that those 15 men -- those 15 members of Serbian forces have established the prisons. This is not what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question was the Serb government, not the members of the special units.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can just check the exact question on LiveNote. I have to go to the case manager on the other side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: If I can be of assistance, Mr. Re, I think I've found your question on page 54, line 16.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The question I asked you, Mr. Sarkanovic, I said, in relation to setting up the facilities for detention, I said someone must have done so, mustn't they. You said: "I don't think I can answer like that. The facilities had been prepared, the secondary school was empty, the TO building was empty and someone had to. That's right. But if you ask me, it was Stevan Todorovic because he was the one who was most frequently ordering arrest. The commandos, members of the special units did it on their own initiative or they had agreed with him to do that. I don't think any facilities had been specially prepared for that. They were as they were, and at the time they happened to be empty." That was the question and answer you had given. If I've -- just hang on. If I've -- I apologise if I slightly misphrased it. What I'm suggesting to you is the 15 to 30 commandos could not have set up these facilities by themselves. It must have been the Serb authorities -- please let me finish -- in control of Bosanski Samac municipality after the takeover, because it would have been physically impossible for 15 to 30 people to do so.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your question, whether it was the Serb authorities, I said yes. But at the same time, I said that arrests were being carried out on orders by Stevan Todorovic and by members of the special units on their own initiative. That was my answer, and I think that was originally your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we agree, then, that these three, on your account, or four, on the evidence in the case, detention facilities could only have been established and maintained and the prisoners looked after by the Serb authorities in control of Bosanski Samac in coordination with Stevan Todorovic?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, these detention centres which you agree could only have been established by the Serb authorities, in conjunction with Stevan Todorovic, allowed beatings, torture, and brutal treatment of detainees, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such treatment was indeed meted out. Now, whether the authorities knew about it or not, I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This system which allowed the establishment of these detention centres which housed hundreds of non-Serbs also allowed Muslim women, children, and Croats women and children to be rounded up and detained at different times, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Everyone working in the police station, that's the SUP, in Bosanski Samac, in April and May and June 1992 was aware of this system of arrest, detention, and mistreatment of the non-Serb prisoners, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: More or less, everyone. Some of them had even been involved in this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Only Serbs worked in the police station?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There were people who belonged to other ethnicities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After April the 17th, 1992, only Serbs were entrusted with the interrogation of Muslim and Croat prisoners?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The two of us interviewed, and we are Serb, so that's what it seems to be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, there weren't any other -- there weren't any Muslim or Croat interrogators working from the Bosanski Samac police station interrogating the non-Serb prisoners while you were working there in April, May, and June 1992, were there?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there weren't any inspectors of different ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The statements that you were taking were taken to assist the Serb authorities in Bosanski Samac, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, by the army, because we talked about the circumstances about gathering the information in relation to army security, that is, arming, establishing of military units, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is in relation -- I withdraw that. Your war assignment was to assist with work at the Bosanski Samac police station from about the 20th of April onwards, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to work. Whether that was some kind of assistance or not, I don't know. My obligation was to work, and I did work. I did my job. My job was, most of the time, to conduct interviews with detainees.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Serb authorities or forces had control of the Bosanski Samac police station at the time you worked there, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if we take into consideration that Stevan Todorovic, at the time, was a member of the Crisis Staff, then of course that is so. They did have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were, of course, aware at the time that Stevan Todorovic was a member of that Crisis Staff. That's when you were working there. Weren't you?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Milos Savic was also aware that Stevan Todorovic was a member of the Crisis Staff at that time, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I presume.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Cancarevic as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Now I object, because this is calling --

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I didn't object the first time, but Mr. Milos Savic and Savo Cancarevic could have known whether Mr. Todorovic was a member, I mean, this is not the witness. He had to speculate what they could possibly know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's a long way and a short way of getting the answer. The witness either knows or he doesn't know. If he says I presume, well, that's the answer I'm stuck with. I could take him through every answer, but I'm not going to. I'm not pushing it any further than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re. When you get the answers, whether or not you are satisfied with them, it's up to you to deal with the witness the best way. Because you know what you want to get out of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: May it please the Court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Zaric, with whom you worked closely, he of course was aware that Mr. Todorovic was a member of the Crisis Staff, and of course it's in his statements to the -- hang on. Hang on -- it's in his statements to the Prosecutor which are in evidence that he was aware at the time that Todorovic was a member of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A moment ago I said I knew, and as I knew, in the same way, Simo Zaric, Cancarevic, and Savic, they could have known, just like myself, and I did know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Stevan Todorovic was a much feared person in the police station and in Bosanski Samac at the time, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how he behaved. It's perhaps more the commandos, because he was practically always socialising with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was closely associated, as far as you could see, with the people who had taken control of the town and were torturing detainees in detention centres, and that made you and other people fear him, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also feared him in your work at the police station, not only because you had heard that he wanted you dead but because of his connection with the Crisis Staff, which was the highest organ of government in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. If I may answer slightly more elaborate way. I stayed out of the way of Stevan Todorovic because of some things that predate this period, and it has nothing to do with him being a member of the Crisis Staff and so on. But in all the ways imaginable, I avoided being anywhere near him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want to take you back to the statements I was asking you about a few moments ago before we moved on to that. When you received your war assignment and turned up at the police station and were told that you had to assist in the taking of statements, it soon became apparent to you that the statements you were taking were directed only at one side, that is, the non-Serbs, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, because I saw that the detained persons were Muslims and Croats. I think that there was one Serb, but he was released very quickly. I don't know who intervened. It was a certain man called Dragan Mesar. I don't know how he was released, but he was released.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the statements that you were taking could be used to assist the Serb authorities and Serb forces in control of Bosanski Samac, couldn't they?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They could have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that is, in fact, the purpose of you being directed to take these statements, because there's no other reason why you would have been asked to take statements from the non-Serbs in custody?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday I said that this was so, that the purpose of the interview was to gather information about the establishment of paramilitary units, that is, units established by the SDA and HDZ, and their arming.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was to assist the Serb authorities and Serb forces in control of Bosanski Samac, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can draw the conclusion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you give the Trial Chamber any other conclusion as to what these statements could have been used for in those circumstances? Because I suggest there's no other.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we can agree that is the only logical conclusion from the work you were directed to do in the Bosanski Samac police station?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can say that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when I said "you," that of course also applies to the other people who were taking statements from the Serb -- non-Serb detainees, such as Mr. Savic, and Mr. Zaric, or Mr. Zaric. Do you not understand the question?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zaric didn't take interviews. I said yesterday he only took one statement, but he read the statements that we took in order to process all this information together with Milos. So it was only Milos Savic and I who took statements.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I've just asked you a number of questions about the system which was in place in Bosanski Samac after the 17th of April, 1992, and you have agreed that the system, in the hands of the Serb forces, in control of Bosanski Samac, allowed mass arrest, detention, torture, of non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that this was happening, but I wasn't aware whether this was known by the Crisis Staff and whether they allowed this. I presume that they knew this because Stevan Todorovic was a member of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you about the system in place. You agreed - I'm just trying to summarise what you said to move on - you've agreed that there was a system in place in Bosanski Samac after April 1992 that allowed mass arrest, torture, detention and mistreatment of non-Serbs? Do you agree with that? I can move on to the next question.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't agree with that system, did you?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you found yourself unwittingly caught up in that system at the Bosanski Samac police station, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that in this way: It was through Milos Savic, in fact, through Milos Bogdanovic, who at the time, Secretary for National Defence, tried to somehow get another assignment, but it probably was not possible or perhaps somebody didn't want to do it so. That's how I stayed there until the 13th of June.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've already agreed you didn't agree with the system. I'm just saying to you that it was a system you didn't agree with, but you found yourself unfortunately and unwittingly caught up in for several months, between April about 20th and mid-June 1992. I'm just suggesting you found yourself caught in this system which was occurring in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't agree with what was being done in SUP and the surrounding area, and I certainly found myself in this spot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "in this spot," you found yourself unwittingly, against your will, because it wasn't your idea to work there, working in that system which was then occurring in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not even near that. I explained how I got there. 19th of April, in the morning, a soldier came for me, told me that I had to report to SUP. When I arrived, they told me --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's not what I'm asking you, sir. We understand how you got there. When you got there, you found, to your horror, there was this terrible system in place, and you had found yourself working in that terrible system and you wanted to get out of it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. Yes, yes, you can say that, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because everyone who was working in that police station was part of that terrible system, whether they wanted to be there or not, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was obvious to you, as a man -- an educated man with a law degree and many years in the police and awareness of laws, that there was a system of persecution being developed against the non-Serbs in Bosanski Samac, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you can say that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you didn't want to be part of this system of persecution, did you?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that, sir, is why you did your utmost to get out of that police station and being part of that system of persecution, wasn't it, because you didn't want to have anything to do with it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I wanted to help these people, even if it was just speaking to them nicely when I did speak to them. But at the same time, I was trying to find out about the possibility of leaving, of getting out of there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's because you disagreed with this system of persecution and you wanted to have no part in it, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that ten times already.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you said earlier in your examination, when Mr. Lazarevic asked you some questions, about one of the reasons that you left was because of what Todorovic was doing and that Todorovic had told you or hinted, or told you that prisoners had to be beaten and force used. That was the evidence you gave before the break.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said --

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said that Mr. Todorovic said that to you. Did he say it -- I'm sorry? I think you just said yes.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yes. I said yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he say that, as far as you can recall, to Mr. Zaric in your presence? Was Mr. Zaric there when Mr. Todorovic said that to you?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I can't really say. Mr. Todorovic told me that on two or three occasions. Well, I don't think he needed to say that to Mr. Zaric, because Mr. Zaric was not doing these jobs that I was, and Mr. Todorovic was not in a position to give orders to Mr. Zaric.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A little bit earlier, Her Honour Judge Williams asked you some questions in relation to the primary school. I just want the usher to show you --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- Exhibit P14A, 49 -- photographs number 49 and 59. If Mr. Usher could just put them on the ELMO in front of you for a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was the building of the primary school. On the right-hand side is the gym.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sarkanovic, just so we all know what you're looking at, can you please look at photograph P14A 49.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do Your Honours have the photos there in front of you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's the primary school, isn't it? The photo on the ELMO there, that's the primary school? You have to answer.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the left-hand side of the photo, is that the primary school? There's a burnt-out building on the left.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's also the primary school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on the right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In front, and left. On the right-hand side is also primary school, but the gym of the primary school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The photo has a date on it of the 6th of October, 1996. You can see from that that it's not burnt out, can't you?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see it now. But I think it is. Believe me, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you --

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, it had burned, and I thought that had burned to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please turn to number 59, ten photos on, which is an interior shot of the same building.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't say anything to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I say to you that this is an agreed photo amongst all the parties here of the interior of the primary school gym, taken in October 1996, if you look at that, it's clearly not a burnt-out building, is it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there's no reason for me not to believe you, but I've already said: I thought this was a burnt-out building, and now I can see that one part of it has not burnt. Because I know that the primary school, after the initial events, the teaching went on in private houses, from which I drew my conclusions, but I didn't go there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I wasn't trying to trick you. I was just trying to clarify that. So when you said earlier the primary school was burnt out, it was just a failure of your memory in relation to which part of the school was burnt out; is that a fair summary of it, being ten years ago?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that my memory failed, but I thought the entire school had burnt down, and now I can see that it hadn't. So I don't doubt your words at all and now I see this is so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Re, can we move on. We've spent too much time on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I thought I was clarifying something from the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Actually, it was more that I had a recollection of those photographs in my mind already.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: May it please the Court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sarkanovic, you were, in 1992, a very experienced -- although retired, very experienced police inspector, and you were very experienced in interrogation techniques, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course. That would be normal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your evidence was that you obtained -- or your police station had a record for obtaining "enviously good results" in the years that you were working there. That was your evidence yesterday.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's certain. That's certain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And for a confession to be --

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just want to add: I don't mean my own, but the results for the crime department on the level of the Republic, when I said that, I didn't mean my personal contribution, although undeniably, it was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, of course you had been working with Dragan Lukac for some time, so you're including him in one of the people who helped you or collectively to obtain those "enviously good results," weren't you?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. Lukac was a good policeman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your experience with your law degree and your work as a police inspector, over many years, has taught you that for a confession or statement taken from a suspect or another person to be of any use to the legal system, it must be voluntary?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in your time as a police inspector, you didn't obtain your "enviously good results" by obtaining confessions or statements after people being tortured, did you?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, certainly not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because the proper procedures, according to law, must be followed in interviewing, interrogating, and taking statements from people, mustn't they?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when a person is in police custody, they are in a vulnerable position vis-a-vis the people who are detaining him or her, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And a confession or a statement taken after a person has been beaten or tortured or sexually assaulted in custody or subjected to inhumane conditions won't be a voluntary or a reliable one, will it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Certainly has an influence on the giving of the statement, but even if such circumstances, even then the statement can be given in good faith, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, if a person has been held without charge in police custody and subjected to daily beatings, underfed, not given proper -- not given bedding to sleep on, toilets to go to, crowded into small conditions and then taken out for an interrogation, you would agree that the statement -- you would agree that that's not done in ideal circumstances, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with that, that it was not taken in ideal circumstances. It was taken as it was taken, and I can say that each person that was interviewed by Milos Savic and by myself --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm asking you: Based upon your experience, as an experienced police inspector and with a law degree and the admission into evidence of statements and confessions taken in police custody - I'm asking you based upon your experience - if someone has been beaten in police custody and is then taken to be interviewed and gives a statement, there will be real questions about its voluntariness or its reliability, if the person has been beaten immediately before giving a statement, won't there? Just as a general proposition.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can say that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if someone -- if people have been arrested and detained, and you've already given evidence that people were detained only because they were non-Serbs, and beaten daily, then taken up for interrogation, the mere fact that they were being interrogated by a -- I withdraw that. Those people in custody were frightened and intimidated, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They were frightened and intimidated because they had been arrested and beaten in detention and kept there, arrested only because they were non-Serbs; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you couldn't say that. First of all, most of them were detained in order to sort out their weapons and the fact that they belonged to units that were established. Only a part of the non-Serbs had been detained without being armed and without belonging to those units.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's 12.30, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. We may proceed, because we're stopping at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: We're stopping -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We can proceed a little more.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: If the Court pleases. We're stopping at 1.00?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We've supposed to stop at 1.00, subject to the tape being changed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll take you away for the moment for the reasons for the detention and just go to the circumstances of the detention of these people in the Bosanski Samac police station in April, May, and June 1992. Your evidence has been of these people being arrested, detained, and severely beaten in police custody.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not all of them, but yes, there were such cases of severe beatings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You, of course, and you've already told us, you interviewed maybe 50 to a hundred of the prisoners who were in detention in the police station, and from the other detention centres; right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Many of those people who you interviewed had been beaten in police custody, hadn't they?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they had been beaten by Serb police and Serb paramilitaries or specials, hadn't they, and Stevan Todorovic, as far as you are aware?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only assume that. I didn't exactly watch as they were beating people, or only very few. But they were the only ones who had unlimited access to prisoners, so only they could have beaten those prisoners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's the only conclusion you could have drawn in those circumstances, isn't it, that they were the ones doing the beating?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the only conclusion. Which other conclusion would you like me to draw?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These people who were beaten by Serbs, these non-Serbs being beaten by Serbs were then interrogated or asked questions by you and other people who were Serb interviewers? You've already agreed to that.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that police inspectors, Milos Savic and myself, those were the police inspectors, and only the two of us conducted interviews. And certainly we conducted interviews with prisoners who had been beaten too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The interrogation of a person of non-Serb ethnicity who had beaten -- been beaten by Serbs, interrogation of that person by a Serb would be intimidating to them in those circumstances, wouldn't it: Arrest, beating, detention, torture by Serbs, taken up for interrogation by a Serb, that would be intimidating to a person in those circumstances, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree with that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If a witness has given evidence here of being beaten immediately before you interrogated them, you wouldn't know whether they had been beaten immediately before, because you weren't there, would you?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I noticed marks of beating on people we interviewed. I didn't know whether they had been beaten immediately before they were brought to me, or maybe two or three days earlier. But one thing is certain: These persons, when they left my office, they were certainly a lot calmer than when they first came to my office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not suggesting they weren't. What I'm asking you is: The person has testified that they were beaten immediately before you interrogated them, you would agree, wouldn't you, that the fact of interrogation by a Serb, after beatings by Serbs, would be intimidating for that person, no matter how gentle you wanted to be with them?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I object. In a general way of asking it, implying beaten by Serbs and brought by Serbs. It's a general question that my colleague could ask, or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So what's wrong with it? There's nothing wrong with the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, there is testimony in this case of people you have interrogated saying they were beaten immediately before. I'm asking you, based on your experience of many years as a police officer and your law degree and so on, that a person who has been beaten immediately before an interrogation and has been beaten by Serbs, after being subjected to horrific conditions you've described, would be intimidated by the mere fact of interrogation by a Serb, no matter how gentle you, as the Serb, were trying to be with them. You would have to agree with that, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's only natural. In other words, I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, we'll move on. So in those circumstances I've just described to you, the Serbian interrogator would not need to use force to obtain a statement or a confession from such a person, would they?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you: Even in addition to things being as you said they were, not all of those who gave statements --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just concentrate on the question I'm asking you, please. I'm confining it to that. Now, a person in those circumstances I've just described, and you've agreed with, that they would naturally be intimidated, the Serbian interrogator would not need to use force to obtain a statement or a confession, would they?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A person in those circumstances may sign anything if they thought it would get them out of there; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only theorise about this, but that's not how it really worked. There were prisoners who didn't state that they had taken part in paramilitary units, although their names were on the lists, the list that had been found. So the statement was drawn up exactly the way the person said things. Sometimes it was not the way it had looked at first. Just because a person's name had been on a list of self-organised citizens of Samac for the defence, specifically.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, a person brought up from police custody, overcrowded, brutal police custody, for an interrogation, would be frightened, even if they had not been beaten before, wouldn't they?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, frightened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because they wouldn't know what's going to happen when they're taken from the cells below or the rooms below, where they've been kept in overcrowded, horrific conditions, they wouldn't know what's going to happen when they're taken out for an interrogation, would they?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And every person in those circumstances taken from the rooms or the cells upstairs, or wherever, to be interviewed or interrogated was in a vulnerable and frightened state, weren't they, everyone?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In theory, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not saying -- not in theory, but you know they were, weren't they, no matter how polite or gentle or nice -- let me finish -- or nice to them you were, you know that the people in detention in that police station, when they were taken for the interview with you, were frightened and vulnerable because of what had happened to them or they had seen happen to other people?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've said that, didn't I?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. You said: "In theory."

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said that. I said this earlier, ten times at least. They were frightened. They had been beaten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whether or not they had been beaten, this is what I'm asking you, and I'm concentrating on this point. The mere fact of their detention in those circumstances would mean that they were vulnerable when they came for their interview, wouldn't it, and in fact it did, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably. I can't really say what some of them may have thought or felt, but I assume that they were frightened, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think you've already agreed the people in those circumstances are more likely to sign things that may not be reliable or may not be voluntary than those who are questioned under ideal conditions according to the rule of law. You agree with that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And of course, the rule of law is very important in the work that you did, both as a police inspector and in the three or the two months that you worked in the Bosanski Samac police station, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because you are in a special position of authority in relation to those in detention whom you are interviewing, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you, as the -- you, plural, being the authorities responsible for detention, custody, interrogation, interviewing, and so on, of people generally - sorry - of people, can only act according to law?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We, and I mean Milos Savic and myself, were in charge of interviewing people, but not in charge of detaining people. Otherwise I fully agree with you in what you said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because the laws of any civilised system regulate detention, custody, police powers of questioning, charging, arrest on bail, and so on, don't they?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the laws cannot be applied arbitrarily or capriciously to people, otherwise it would violate the principle -- which you would have learned in law school and applied in practice -- of the rule of law?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And crimes must also be clearly defined for someone such as yourself, a police inspector, to have the power to investigate them?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In April 1992, May and June of 1992, you were taking statements from detainees in relation to, you say, arming activities. That's what you generally, broadly say. I want to move on to something. You agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As of the 7th of April, 1992, the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina had been recognised internationally by the European Community, the United States, and the next day, the 8th, it changed its name to the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The legitimate and internationally recognised government of the entire territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, as of the 17th of April, 1992, was the Republic -- was the government of the state of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Re, that's not a question for this witness. I know that he has said that he's a lawyer, but this is beyond what this witness can answer to.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'll ask it another way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: He hasn't come here as an expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'll take it in another direction. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sarkanovic, I've already asked you about the laws and the facts --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Re, I understand the tape is being rewound. Maybe we can wait for two minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'll certainly do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You can proceed, Mr. Re. You can proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When I started, I showed you Mr. Zaric's record of interview, in which he said or told the Prosecutors that all three parties or ethnic groups were arming themselves in Bosanski Samac area in April 1992. Now, you commenced your work on the 20th of April, 1992, working in the Serb-controlled police station --

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 19th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The 19th. I correct myself. The 19th of April, 1992, working in the Serb-controlled police station. You've told us that you were interviewing non-Serbs in relation to arming by the HDZ and the SDA. You've already agreed that, as a police inspector or someone working in a police station in relation to people in police custody, that you must act according to the rule of law. My question is: You must know, to do that, what the laws are that you are applying, as a police inspector, mustn't you?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You must be -- to do your job properly, you must be intimately familiar with the precise sections of the Penal Code, the breaches of which you are investigating, mustn't you?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Penal Code, yes. The Law on Criminal Procedure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Between the 19th of April, 1992 and the day in June that just slips my mind for a moment, I think it was the 12th of June, 1992, when you left the Bosanski police?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 13th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The 13th of June, 1992, under what law were you interviewing these people in police custody?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Re, again, this is not a question for this witness. These are the matters we are saying that they're not for fact witnesses. These are matters four your submissions, as to what law was in force.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm not asking the witness what law was in force. The witness has given evidence of being a police inspector.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Of respecting the rule of law, of only being able to ask questions of people in police custody according to the rule of law and the laws in force. All I'm asking him is: Under what law was he acting when he interviewed these witnesses? He may be able to tell us. I'm not asking him what law was in force. I'm asking him what law did he personally apply. That's as far as I'm taking it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you understand the question? What law were you acting under --

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Law on Criminal Procedure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which one was that? Of what entity?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the former Yugoslavia ceased to exist on the 27th of April, 1992, when Serbia and Montenegro declared themselves to be the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and renounced any territorial claims to the territory of Bosnia, what law were you acting under after the 27th of April, between the 27th of April and the 12th of June --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Re, yes, again, this is a problem here. This is not for this witness to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may. We have very solid evidence in this case, and there were many of witnesses who controlled this and being asked what was the laws that were applied. And we do have evidence that the same laws that were in force in Yugoslavia, Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, were adopted during war, in both entities of Bosnia and Herzegovina. There was not any differences between law that were applied in the Federation, in the Muslim-controlled territories, Croatian-controlled territories and Serb-controlled territories within Bosnia-Herzegovina during whole war. So there is absolutely no base for this question. There are two basic laws: Criminal law and criminal proceedings. The laws that were applied on the whole territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina during the whole war.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can I deal with it this way? I'll just ask this witness of fact, which law he was acting under at all times, as a witness of fact, which is the law he thought he was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Dealing with, applying himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said the laws of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Can you just tell us which --

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. The criminal --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which code, and if you can remember which section, just as best as you can do.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The law on criminal proceed and the Penal Code.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I think he had answered that question before, if you check line 20, I think 79, line 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I was just trying to clarify it was at all times, even after the 20th of April. But I'm satisfied with the clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The answer as to which law he himself was personally complying with.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. It goes off the screen. That's the trouble. And I lose the question and forget what it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Sarkanovic, the -- as far as you were aware, in your knowledge of criminal procedure and the codes you had been applying or working under, the Federal Republic Criminal Code didn't authorise the mass arrest of people on ethnic grounds, did it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said before: I did not arrest people. I merely interviewed them. There were other people in charge of arresting people, and on other people's orders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I was asking you based upon your work, your familiarity with the Criminal Code, having worked under it for many years, as far as you can recall, it didn't authorise the mass arrest of people on ethnic grounds, did it? Just the code.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. Although the law doesn't specify the number of people who are or are not to be arrested.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The code, as it was then applied, didn't authorise the arrest of people on political grounds either, did it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nor the detention of people only on political grounds?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Under the condition that no criminal act was committed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sulejman Tihic, your evidence yesterday, was you interviewed him and your position was he had committed no crime and should be free to leave, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because you certainly had no evidence that he had committed any offence against the Criminal Code, and you're investigating offences against the Criminal Code; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't read Sulejman Tihic's statement specifically, but I believe not. All those statements were later to be sent for assessment as to whether a criminal act had been committed or not, in order to then be further processed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You recommended the release of Sulejman Tihic because, from everything you had seen, there was no evidence that he had committed any offence against the Criminal Code; correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Simo Zaric proposed to Stevan Todorovic that he be released, and my suggestion was, once the proposal was not adopted and when Stevan Todorovic refused to release Sulejman Tihic, I told him that he should hide from members of the Special Forces so that they would no longer mistreat him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sulejman Tihic was a prominent local member of the SDA, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The president, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you had formed your view that he had committed no criminal offence -- no offence against the Criminal Code, it was apparent that he was only being detained on political grounds, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm telling you: I didn't read Mr. Tihic's statement, and as a matter of fact, I don't know what he said in that statement and whether there were indeed any elements of criminal acts. I didn't talk to him, to Sulejman Tihic. I would occasionally enter the room. And all the time that I was inside, we didn't talk about the reason why he had been brought in. It was more, you know, a sort of personal conversation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you had known Mr. Tihic for many years and had worked with him as he was a prosecutor in Bosanski Samac. You must have been interested in the reason for his arrest; yes?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR SARKANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already told you: I was interested, but the statement had been taken by Mr. Zaric, or rather, Mr. Zaric was taking the statement. I went to the conference room and conducted other interviews from other persons. I didn't think it was necessary for me to be there during his interview.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric -- sorry - Mr. Tihic was a prominent SDA -- sorry - prominent SDA politician, political leader, and a prominent lawyer in Bosanski Samac, whom you knew. After you spoke to Mr. Zaric, you formed the view that there was no reason for his continued detention, because he had committed no offence, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I mean, I believe this is -- could you just wait a bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: This is the third time that same question has been posed to the witness, and he said he's not familiar with what Sulejman Tihic said to Mr. Zaric. He wasn't present at the moment. He hasn't read his statement. So whether there were any reasons for Sulejman Tihic to remain in detention or not cannot be familiar to this witness. He can speculate. He may be -- most probably had his own opinion on whether Mr. Tihic was supposed to stay or be released.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The point is that the question --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I don't believe it's for us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The question has been repeated, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I apologise. I'm just looking for something in the transcript in relation to something the witness said about Mr. Tihic this morning which led me to ask that question. I'm just looking for the exact quotation. I'm sorry, Your Honour. I can't find it. I can't immediately locate it. It may have been yesterday. It's 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: It's 1.00, Mr. Re. We shall adjourn now, because there's a Status Conference to be held in this same courtroom. We shall continue our proceedings tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 13th day of March 2003, at 9.00 a.m. 22 23 24 25
